item.content:encoded:
Christina Haack has received another chance at love with Christopher Larocca.
After the pair were spotted on a joint trip to Italy in October 2024 followed by an appearance at Amy Sexton’s holiday party in Laguna Beach, California, in December 2024, Us confirmed in January 2025 that Haack was dating Larocca.
The couple went Instagram official in February 2025, going on to make their red carpet debut in May 2025.
Haack recently went through a public divorce from Hall in July 2024 after over two years of marriage.
“Everyone’s just doing better since he’s gone. Just all that negative energy,” she said during an episode of Christina on the Coast, referring to her children Taylor and Brayden whom she shares with ex Tarek El Moussa and son Hudson whom she shares with ex Ant Anstead. “I truly tried to make that work.”
Keep scrolling to learn more about Haack and Larocca’s relationship:
October 2024
The Daily Mail claimed that Haack and Hall were seen on a trip to Italy together.
December 2024
The pair were spotted at Sexton’s holiday party in Laguna Beach, per Daily Mail.
January 2025
Us confirmed that Haack was dating Larocca, who is the CEO of Network Connex in Orange County, California. Later that month, the couple were spotted at LAX traveling to Paris for Haack’s business trip.
February 2025
Haack and Larocca went Instagram official when she shared a photo of the pair flying on a private plane.
“Some plane flights must be hard,” she captioned the post.
That same month, Haack and Larocca went on a double date with Tarek and his wife, Heather Rae El Moussa.
“First round of interviews ✅,” Tarek shared in an Instagram post.
March 2025
Larocca appeared in the background of The Flip Off’s season finale.
April 2025
Haack shared in an Instagram post about anxious attachment that finding a man “who has his own amazing career, life & hobbies (who also happens to have zero jealousy) can at times feel strange for someone who has had the opposite.”
Later that month, Haack’s ex Tarek told Us that the “double dates” with Larocca and Haack are “actually fun.”
“The new guy she’s dating, I really like him. He’s really nice,” he shared. “Honestly, he just seems like a good guy. She’s going through a really tough situation and, based on my conversations with her, he’s supportive, he’s guiding, he’s experienced and he is giving her good advice.”
May 2025
The couple made their red carpet debut at The Flip Off For Your Consideration Emmy event in Los Angeles.
“A supportive partner > everything,” Haack shared via her Instagram Story.
September 2026
To mark two years of dating, Haack shared a heartfelt appreciation post for Larocca.
“Two years of getting to know you. Together we built a champagne brand from the ground up, partnered on a flip for tv (coming soon) and traveled to amazing places,” she wrote via Instagram on September 21. “I have watched you handle everything with grace and understanding and therefore you have taught me to do the same. Thank you for making my life EASY. What a true gift that is. A gift I would not have appreciated in my younger years. Taking things slow and not rushing through life is something I also can greatly appreciate in my 40s. Thank you for being a true partner in all the ways @cml949 🤍.”

item.content:encoded:
If you’ve ever wondered why you’re perfectly chill when someone you’re dating takes three hours to text back while your best friend is already drafting a “so I guess you hate me?” follow-up after 20 minutes, attachment styles might have something to do with it. Or maybe you’re the one who starts feeling vaguely trapped the second someone gets a little too close. Also potentially an attachment thing!
Basically, attachment styles describe some of the ways we navigate emotional connections with other people. “Attachment theory sheds light on how humans form and maintain emotional bonds,” explains relationship and EMDR therapist Ashley Starwood, LCSW. The theory, originally developed by psychologists John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth, suggests that our earliest relationships with parents or caregivers can influence how we approach relationships later in life.
There are four main attachment styles: secure, anxious, avoidant, and disorganized (also known as fearful-avoidant). And while figuring out yours might explain a thing or two about why you act the way you do when feelings get involved, it’s not a diagnosis or some permanent relationship fate you’re stuck with forever. You can even experience different attachment patterns with different people.
So, yes, there may actually be a reason you’re drawn to people who make you want to throw your phone into the ocean. Ahead, experts break down what each attachment style means, where it comes from, how it can affect your relationships, and whether you can change yours.
How Are Attachment Styles Formed?
Attachment styles are largely shaped by early childhood experiences. “Your parents’ ability to be attuned to your needs and be emotionally safe caregivers greatly impacts your ability to build secure attachment,” says Morgan Anderson, PsyD, an attachment theory expert and author of Love Magnet. For example, caregivers who consistently and compassionately meet their child’s needs can help foster a sense of trust. “Conversely, inconsistent, neglectful, or even abusive caregiving can create feelings of insecurity, anxiety, or fear in the child,” adds Starwood.
But your parents or caregivers aren’t the only relationships that can shape your attachment patterns. Anderson says early non-familial relationships can play a role, too, and experiences later in life can also affect how you approach relationships. According to eharmony’s September 2023 Dating Diaries report, for example, 84 percent of Gen Z singles said past heartbreaks had made them “more cautious” about relationships, while 72 percent said they’d become “less trusting,” notes eharmony relationship expert Laurel House.
Your attachment style isn’t necessarily identical in every relationship, either. You might feel more secure with some people and more anxious, avoidant, or fearful-avoidant with others. Your partner’s attachment style can influence the dynamic between you, as can your current circumstances and feelings of self-worth.
Secure Attachment
As the name suggests, someone with a secure attachment style generally feels, well, secure in forming and maintaining healthy relationships. They tend to value closeness in their relationships, Anderson explains, but also know how to set healthy boundaries and communicate their needs effectively. “In securely-attached relationships, partners experience ‘interdependence,’ meaning they are able to practice self-soothing simultaneously and can also ask their partner for support and reassurance,” she says.
How it’s formed: House says caregivers who are consistently present and responsive to their child’s needs within the first year of life and beyond can help foster secure attachment.
Anxious Attachment
While someone with an anxious attachment style may crave closeness with their partner, Starwood says they often have a deep-seated fear of abandonment and rejection. They may frequently seek reassurance from their partners but struggle to actually believe or internalize it when they get it.
“With anxious attachment, there is often coping through excessive communication, becoming a ‘chameleon’ in your relationships, passive expression of needs, and even codependency,” Anderson explains. “Unconsciously, the anxiously attached person is thinking, I will do anything not to be abandoned.”
How it’s formed: “Emotionally inconsistent and unpredictable caregivers contribute to creating adults with anxious relationships,” says House. Parents who are sometimes available and sometimes distant can lead to children (and eventually, adults) who feel anxious about future connections.
Avoidant Attachment
Think of avoidant attachment as pretty much the polar opposite of anxious attachment. Instead of craving constant reassurance, someone with an avoidant attachment style tends to value hyper-independence and may feel uncomfortable with closeness. “If you have an avoidant attachment style, you struggle to be vulnerable in your relationships and may find yourself pulling away from people,” Anderson explains. “Avoidantly-attached individuals still crave intimacy, but their fear of it outweighs their desire to be close. There is often a lack of emotional awareness with avoidant attachment, meaning these individuals are not connected to their own emotional experience, which in turn makes it nearly impossible for them to connect to the emotional experience of others.”
How it’s formed: Dismissive, disconnected, or distant caregiving can contribute to avoidant attachment, House says. When children’s emotional needs aren’t consistently met within their relationships, they may learn to rely primarily on themselves.
Disorganized Attachment
The final attachment style is disorganized, also known as fearful-avoidant (FA), and according to Anderson, it’s often linked to childhood trauma. “An individual with an FA attachment style experiences both anxious and avoidant strategies simultaneously,” she says. “This can manifest as a pendulum swinging from fear of abandonment to desiring complete independence. Those with a fearful-avoidant attachment style have a hard time trusting anyone and struggle to form lasting relationships.”
How it’s formed: Disorganized attachment can develop in highly unpredictable or abusive environments. “Fearful-avoidant attachment is characterized by inconsistent or unpredictable caregiving experiences,” Starwood explains. “It involves a mix of behaviors, where a child might seek closeness but then become withdrawn or fearful, reflecting the instability they experience at home.”
How to Figure Out Your Attachment Style
Maybe one of those descriptions just gave you a major lightbulb moment. Or maybe you read all four and are still sitting here like, okay, but which one am I? If you’re not sure, Starwood suggests reflecting on your childhood, experiences with caregivers, and past relationships, paying attention to how each may have affected your sense of security and trust.
There are also online tests that can help you explore your attachment style. You can try this attachment style quiz from the Attachment Project or Anderson’s five-minute attachment style questionnaire. Whichever you take, Starwood stresses that the results should be considered a starting point rather than a definitive answer.
“A psychotherapist can provide a more in-depth assessment of your attachment style using standardized tools and clinical interviews,” she says. “This can be particularly helpful if you're interested in a deeper understanding of your attachment patterns and how they might impact your relationships.”
How to Change Your Attachment Style
Good news: Your attachment style isn’t set in stone. Even if certain patterns have been with you since childhood, it’s possible to develop healthier, more secure ways of relating to other people. The first step, Anderson says, is understanding the patterns you tend to fall into. “It starts with awareness, followed by actively releasing outdated patterns through emotional regulation and secure relationship skills like assertive communication and setting boundaries.”
Therapy can also help, says Starwood, especially if you’re trying to understand where certain patterns come from and develop new ways of responding to them. Depending on what you’re working through, that might mean learning to communicate your needs more directly, set boundaries, regulate difficult emotions, or feel more comfortable with intimacy.
And don’t expect your attachment patterns to change overnight. “Celebrate your progress, no matter how small, and be patient with yourself,” Starwood says. Becoming more secure is less about suddenly transforming into a completely different person and more about noticing old patterns and gradually learning how to respond differently.
Ultimately, knowing your attachment style isn’t about putting yourself into a box. It’s about understanding yourself—and your relationships—a little better, then deciding what, if anything, you’d like to do differently going forward.

item.content:encoded:
Secure Attachment and Youth Loneliness
The role of secure attachment in preventing loneliness and misuse of social media.

Posted September 14, 2026 Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
Key points
- Secure attachments are essential for cognitive, social, and emotional well-being.
- Secure attachments prevent loneliness in young people by fostering bonding with others and social skills.
- Research shows that secure attachments help prevent social media addiction and digital media misuse.
- Parents can learn skills for establishing secure attachments in early life and throught the life cycle.
All the lonely people/Where do they all come from/All the lonely people/Where do they all belong
Lennon and McCartney
With Gen Z now reporting the highest rates of loneliness of any generation, and parents more concerned than ever about the perils of social media amid recent suits against META, researchers and clinicians are increasingly pointing to something we’ve understood for decades: the power of a secure, trusting bond between a child and the adults who raise them.
In the psychological literature, they appear to be crucial for:
- Effective and accurate cognitive functions
- Emotional flexibility
- Feeling safer and more secure
- Finding meaning in experiences
- Self-regulation and managing one’s own feelings and behaviors
- The capacity for intimacy and healthy interpersonal relationships
- Empathy
- Self-awareness and comfort with one’s identity
- Resilience
That’s a lot, and more than any parent or caregiver could possibly want for our kids, teens, and young adults. Kids with secure attachments tend to handle stress better, bounce back from setbacks, form closer friendships, and know themselves more clearly.
But how does this happen?
We humans are pack animals. We need each other. We need relationships.
As Winnicott so clearly pointed out, development requires both a biological endowment and a facilitating environment. The former is rooted in genetics and physical contributions to our development, and the second, perhaps most important part of our life experience, is rooted in relationships.
Dan Siegel summarized the process well. It is a gradual process, beginning and grounded in the first three years of life. Its components include:
- Collaborative Communication: Parental attunement to the child
- Reflective Dialogue: Creating the sense that subjective experience is important and can be shared. This allows the child to be seen
- Repair: Identification and repair of miscommunications and misunderstandings. This requires that both parent and child are mindful of breaches, and use apology and reparations, to mend fences
- Emotional Communication: Sharing and amplifying the positive and mitigating the negative in the interpersonal world of parent and child
- Developing Coherent Narratives: Helping the child and teen develop an internal autobiographical sense of self, and self-awareness, key for self-reflection and a solid sense of identity
Attachment theory has shaped how we understand social and emotional development, parenting, and our own relational patterns. Yet little research addresses how secure attachment protects against specific, longstanding threats to youth development.
In particular, let’s consider loneliness and misuse of social media.
Secure Attachment and Loneliness
On May 3, 2023, The United States Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy released a new Advisory calling attention to the public health crisis of loneliness, isolation, and lack of connection in our country.
According to the Advisory, social connection is a critical but underappreciated contributor to individual overall health, community safety, and resilience. Yet, around half of all U.S. adults report experiencing loneliness, with some of the highest rates among our young people. In fact, today the Gen Z population reports the highest rates of loneliness.
The Surgeon General noted that it is important to “Invest in your relationship with your child or loved one by recognizing that strong, secure attachments are protective and a good foundation for other healthy relationships.”
The report didn’t specify how to foster these attachments (practical examples follow below.) There have been some studies (though few) on how secure attachment mitigates loneliness.
Consider a teenager who gets left out of a group chat, or shows up to find plans have changed without them. A securely attached teen is more likely to mention it to a parent that night, or reach out to another friend, rather than sitting with it alone and assuming the worst about themselves.
Teenagers’ needs for bonding with others, feeling fulfilled, and trust are grounded in their secure attachment profile. As such, they are more likely to seek help and support when distressed, rather than worrying alone. Their sense of connection to others also helps them build highly developed social skills, mitigating temporary isolation without it developing into chronic loneliness. Their sense of connection becomes a part of their autobiographical narrative, and is an important outcome of secure attachment.
Secure Attachment and Problematic Social Media Use
Parents, caregivers, clinicians, and legislators alike have grown concerned about digital media because of both its habit-forming design, and the way young people can misuse it, for instance, for bullying, excessive texting, or ghosting.
Though research is limited, evidence suggests that secure attachments reduce vulnerability to digital media misuse. One study linked insecure attachment to social media addiction, with social support outside of media use acting as a mediator. Another study found secure attachment associated with less addiction and fewer mental health problems.
Secure attachments can reduce a young person’s need to look to social media for validation, emotional regulation, and relief from negative emotions.
None of this means social media is inherently harmful—for many young people, it’s a genuine source of connection and community. The point is more specific: When a young person already feels secure and connected, they’re less likely to depend on a device to meet needs the device can’t fulfill.
What Can Parents and Caregivers Do
With Siegel’s framework in mind, here are some guidelines for nurturing secure attachment:
- When your child is upset, slow down, get on their level, name their feelings, and match your tone before jumping to solutions.
- Ask an open question about their day, and sit with the whole answer with curiosity, instead of moving straight to advice.
- After a blowup, come back later and name what happened. You might say, “I got too frustrated earlier, and I’m sorry” or something similar. The repair matters more than the rupture.
- Identify and name positive moments aloud in the moment they happen so the good moments register. This could look like, “I love that we laughed about that together,” or “I enjoyed watching that with you.”
- To facilitate narrative building skills, ask your teen to tell you about their day as a story instead of a checklist. For example, try phrases like, “Walk me through your day,” as opposed to “How was school.”
Promoting secure attachments is not easy. For many, Siegel’s skills are complicated by real obstacles: parents’ own insecure attachment histories; adverse childhood experiences; economic pressure; disparities related to race, immigration status, or gender identity; unstable family structure; domestic conflict; or psychiatric or physical disability.
It is imperative to recognize these obstacles and seek support — from family, friends, spiritual leaders, or mental health professionals.
And in the process of getting help, parents and caregivers may not only promote secure attachments with their children but earn secure attachment profiles for themselves.
To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
Also posted in a longer form at the Clay Center for Young Healthy Minds at Massachusetts General Hospital.
